attrs.i2t:evidence: The following register details deceased individuals documented on ICE's official Detainee Death Reporting ledger from Fiscal Year 2024 through late Fiscal Year 2026.

Because these individuals are technically classified as released from physical custody at the time death is pronounced, ICE systematically excludes them from its public Detainee Death Reporting registry.
attrs.ddd:exclusion_mechanism: humanitarian parole / bond release shortly before death

attrs.i2t:evidence: Clinical oversight evaluations coordinated by Physicians for Human Rights (PHR) and the ACLU indicate that these deaths are frequently attributable to chronic failures in correctional healthcare administration.

Investigations conducted by Human Rights Watch under the 'Deported to Danger' project verified 138 killings of Salvadorans deported from the United States, along with more than 70 cases of torture, sexual assault, and enforced disappearance occurring shortly after arrival.

...dedicated Contract Detention Facilities (CDFs) operated by private corrections entities like GEO Group and CoreCivic, Intergovernmental Service Agreements (IGSAs) with local sheriffs, and U.S. Marshals Service (USMS) inter-agency arrangements.
Federal litigation, including J.G.G. v. Trump and D.V.D. v. DHS, demonstrated that detainees were subjected to 23.5-hour solitary confinement in unlit cells.
To circumvent these legal bars, federal enforcement agencies executed third-country agreements that allow noncitizens to be expelled to foreign partner jurisdictions with which they have no ties.
The daily detained population climbed past 65,000 individuals by mid-2026, surpassing the previous historical record of approximately 50,000 to 55,000 set in August 2019.
Cumulative book-ins across the expanded enforcement apparatus reached 591,385, with July 2026 logging more than 46,000 admissions in a single month.
Microdata analyzed by TRAC and the Deportation Data Project confirms that nearly three-quarters of all detained noncitizens have no criminal record (73.6% non-criminal, 48,377 of 65,735).
Under intensified detention policies, 60-day release rates plummeted from 35% to less than 7%.
Interior arrests multiplied by a factor of 11 as agents targeted individuals outside courthouses, at mandatory check-in appointments, and in public settings.
While the agency recorded over 170 deaths across the combined period between 2003 and 2025, custodial deaths exceeded 32 individuals in 2025 alone.
Recent enforcement has disproportionately targeted Haitian immigrants—following the administrative termination of Temporary Protected Status—alongside Venezuelan, Cuban, and African nationals.
Official mortality metrics exclude lethal force encounters occurring during community arrest operations, street sweeps, and residential entries executed by ERO and HSI personnel.
attrs.ddd:exclusion_mechanism: lethal force outside custody; handled as police shooting investigations

attrs.i2t:evidence: When noncitizens are removed from the United States, official domestic monitoring ceases at the border.

Federal tracking of deaths in immigration custody is formally regulated under the DHS Appropriations Act of 2018, which requires ICE to publish reports regarding in-custody deaths within 90 days of occurrence.

The relevant Field Office Director must issue notifications within 12 hours to senior leadership in ERO and OPR; an interim notice must be published within two business days, followed by Mortality Review Reports by IHSC and OPR Detainee Death Reviews, with toxicology and autopsy records finalized within 60 to 180 days.

Physical custody is distributed across 469 facilities nationwide... Crucially, ICE's public directory lists only 208 centers, obscuring more than 260 municipal lockups, county jails, and transit staging facilities from standard visibility.

Even after an immigration judge issues a final removal order, noncitizens retain constitutional and statutory rights to file emergency motions to reopen, seek judicial stays of removal, or petition federal district courts for writs of habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241. By concealing the physical location of detainees... ICE effectively prevents legal counsel and families from serving legal papers, obtaining signatures, or filing emergency pleadings before expulsion.
Under the Privacy Act of 1974 and federal FOIA exemptions (specifically 5 U.S.C. § 552(b)(6) and (b)(7)(C)), ICE routinely redacts names and Alien Numbers from public microdata releases.
While federal courts issued injunctions halting transfers to specific third countries, the Supreme Court permitted removals to continue in late September 2026 while litigation proceeds on the merits.

attrs.ddd:coverage_note: Detainees who die while in official physical ICE detention; excludes deaths post-release or during street-level operations.
Monthly detention census, average daily population, facility criminal profiles, court backlogs; 30-60 day lag.
Raw ICE arrest logs, detention book-in microdata, facility transfers, deportation flight manifests; quarterly to semi-annual releases following court orders.
Federal district court dockets, emergency TRO filings, habeas petitions; real-time indexing, limited to detainees who secure representation.
Facility conditions, solitary confinement abuse, geographic coordinates of detention sites; crowdsourced and visitation-dependent.
Transferred noncitizens, third-country facilities, post-removal violent deaths; investigative cadence, no continuous census.
Manual locator; post-2026-09-15 deliberately returns empty records for final-order detainees.
